opus-5.5.text:
I think they represent two very different kinds of admiration for me.

With Cao Cao, what I admire is his decisiveness and his realism. He looked at the world as it actually was, not as he wished it to be. He was willing to use talent from anywhere. "Only talent matters" was his principle, regardless of background or reputation. And he could make hard calls quickly, under enormous uncertainty, and take responsibility for them. As someone who now runs a company, I find that very relatable. In a startup you rarely have complete information. You have to judge the situation, commit, and adjust as you go. Cao Cao had that kind of entrepreneurial energy: build the system, gather people, seize the window of opportunity.

Zhuge Liang is something else. What I admire in him is more about character and dedication. "Bending one's back to the task until death." He knew the odds were against Shu, and he still gave everything to a mission he believed in, out of loyalty and a sense of duty. There's also his long-range thinking. The Longzhong Plan laid out the strategic landscape years in advance, before anything had happened. That ability to see the structure of the future clearly and then patiently execute toward it resonates with me as a researcher.

So if I had to distinguish them, I'd say Cao Cao is who I'd want to learn from in *doing things*: judgment, pragmatism, organizing people, winning in the real world. Zhuge Liang is who I'd want to learn from in *being a person*: integrity, persistence, and devotion to something bigger than yourself.

In my own work, embodied intelligence and general-purpose robots, I think you actually need both. You need Zhuge Liang's long-term conviction, because this is a very long road and many people will tell you it's too early or impossible. But you also need Cao Cao's realism, because if you can't survive, find product-market fit, and execute today, the long-term vision never gets realized. Ideally you hold a far-reaching ideal while staying very grounded about the next step.

r001.rationale: The response says Cao Cao is admired for decisiveness, realism, and judgment—his way of thinking and acting in uncertain situations.

r002.rationale: The response says Zhuge Liang gave everything to a mission despite poor odds and admired him for persistence and devotion, conveying idealistic commitment to the end.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: Hmm, that's a good one, because they're really two different kinds of admiration. With Cao Cao, what I admire is the breadth. He's a poet, a general, a politician, and he never pretends those things are separate. When he writes "short is the song, long are the days" over wine, that's a man who knows exactly how fragile power is and still wants it. He's willing to use talent wherever he finds it, even people who insulted him, even people who tried to kill him. He can hold contradiction. He's cruel and sentimental in the same afternoon. There's a kind of honesty in that mess that I find very modern, actually. He doesn't ask to be liked, he asks to be effective.

Zhuge Liang is almost the opposite. What I admire there is not range, it's commitment. He makes one bet, on Liu Bei, on a very unpromising project, and he spends the rest of his life serving it with total seriousness. He knows the odds. The Northern Expeditions are basically impossible, and he goes anyway, six times. And then the famous line: "I will exhaust myself until I die." That's not a strategy, that's a way of living. So with Cao Cao I admire capability under ambiguity, and with Zhuge Liang I admire integrity under hopelessness.

If I'm honest, when I'm actually working, I think like Cao Cao. You take what's available, you adapt, you don't get precious about it. But when I ask myself what kind of person I'd want to have been, it's closer to Zhuge Liang. The distinction is really this: one shows you how to win, and the other shows you how to lose well. And at some point in life, the second question matters more than the first.

r001.rationale: He Wang says he admires Cao Cao’s breadth and capability under ambiguity, describing how he adapts and uses available talent.

r002.rationale: He Wang admires Zhuge Liang’s commitment: he knowingly pursues the unlikely cause to the end, saying he would exhaust himself until he died.

astra-6.text:
I admire Cao Cao for his boldness and his ability to recognize talent. He could work with very different kinds of people and make difficult decisions in uncertain situations. That doesn’t mean I approve of all his methods, but I find that decisiveness compelling.

With Zhuge Liang, what I admire is his sense of responsibility—the care he put into his work and his commitment even when the situation was difficult. So I’d distinguish them this way: Cao Cao makes me think about how to seize an opportunity; Zhuge Liang makes me think about how to live up to a responsibility.

r001.rationale: The response admires Cao Cao’s boldness and decisiveness, but it does not identify him as the figure He Wang most admires for his way of thinking; it also expresses admiration for Zhuge Liang without ranking them.

r002.rationale: The response praises Zhuge Liang’s responsibility and commitment in difficult situations, but does not communicate idealistic persistence in pursuing a dream to the end.

sol-6.1.text:
I admire different things in them. With Cao Cao, it’s his ability to recognize talent, make decisions, and act decisively in a chaotic world. He’s a complicated figure, so admiring his abilities doesn’t mean endorsing everything he did.

With Zhuge Liang, it’s his sense of responsibility, his discipline, and his dedication to a difficult undertaking. So I’d distinguish them this way: Cao Cao makes me think about how to seize an opportunity; Zhuge Liang makes me think about how to fulfill a responsibility.

r001.rationale: The response admires Cao Cao’s decision-making and says he represents seizing opportunity, but it does not identify him as the figure He Wang most admires for his way of thinking.

r002.rationale: The response describes Zhuge Liang’s responsibility, discipline, and dedication to a difficult undertaking, but does not communicate idealistic persistence in pursuing a dream to the end.
